headline: Former Yale football coach Tony Reno dies at 52
dek: Reno led Yale to five Ivy League championships and 83 wins during a 14-year tenure that reshaped the Bulldogs’ place in the FCS.
body: Tony Reno, the former Yale football coach who guided the Bulldogs through five Ivy League championships, has died at 52, Yale Athletics announced Friday. The news reached the New Haven campus less than eight months after Reno stepped down from the program for health reasons. The [Yale memorial](https://yalebulldogs.com/news/2026/10/2/in-memoriam-former-football-head-coach-tony-reno.aspx) described a coach whose influence extended beyond wins and losses into the lives of the students he mentored. The Associated Press, in [reporting carried by the Boston Globe](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/10/02/sports/reno-yale-football/), said no cause of death was given.

Reno’s record places him among the most successful coaches in Yale’s long football history. He went 83-49 over 14 seasons, according to Yale and the AP, and ranks second in career victories behind Carm Cozza. His teams won Ivy League titles in 2017, 2019, 2022, 2023 and 2025. Yale also beat Harvard in seven of the final nine meetings under Reno, giving his tenure a particularly strong mark in the rivalry that anchors the program’s season each fall.

The final championship season added a new chapter. Yale’s official account of Reno’s tenure says the 2025 Bulldogs finished 8-2 in the regular season and 6-1 in league play, earning the Ivy League’s first automatic berth in the NCAA Football Championship Subdivision playoffs. Yale then rallied from a 28-point deficit to beat Youngstown State 43-42 in the opening round before losing 21-13 to eventual national champion Montana State. The Bulldogs finished No. 13 in the final FCS rankings. That run gave the program a national stage while preserving the Ivy League’s academic and athletic identity.

Reno left the job in February, when he said his health situation made stepping down the right decision for Yale football. In its [announcement at the time](https://yalebulldogs.com/news/2026/2/17/tony-reno-steps-down-as-head-coach-of-yale-football.aspx), the university said Reno had led the program since January 2012 and had helped establish a foundation for the next coach. He had spent more than a decade on Yale’s staff before becoming head coach, including work under Jack Siedlecki on the 2006 Ivy championship team. Kevin Cahill took over the program after a national search.

The numbers tell only part of why the announcement is significant to Yale and the region. Yale said six Bulldogs won the Asa S. Bushnell Cup as Ivy League Player of the Year during Reno’s tenure, while five Yale players were selected in the NFL Draft over the past seven years covered by the university’s February review. The school also credited Reno’s teams with success in the classroom and community. In its memorial, Yale emphasized his standards for student-athletes and the relationships he built with players, colleagues and alumni rather than presenting the coaching change simply as a succession story.

Reno’s connection to the area ran through both New Haven and Massachusetts. Yale identified him as a Massachusetts native, and the university’s account of his career says he spent his early Yale years as an assistant before returning to lead the Bulldogs. His family remained part of the program’s public story: the AP reported that he is survived by his wife, Toni, and their children, Dante, Angelina and Vince. Dante was Yale’s quarterback during the 2025 championship season, when the Bulldogs made their first FCS postseason appearance.

For Yale, the immediate task is continuing a program that Reno left with a conference title, a playoff win and a clear competitive identity. For New Haven, his death closes the chapter on a coach who spent much of his career tied to the city and its university. Yale’s tribute makes clear what will be measured now: not only how the Bulldogs perform under Cahill, but how much of Reno’s emphasis on mentorship survives in the players who follow him.
author: NorthEast News Desk
